results.summary: This design implements an adder with separate flow control for each argument and the result, using one of several selectable pipeline register or buffer modules. It is a solution to an RTL job interview question described by Yuri Panchul and is used in the educational systemverilog-homework and basics-graphics-music repositories. The design includes a self-checking testbench and can be manually tested with buttons and LEDs to cover back-to-back data, argument starvation, and backpressure. It is an educational design demonstrating different flow control strategies at the RTL level.

results.summary_before: This analog design contains two ring oscillators, one built from 18 inverters and a NAND enable gate targeting roughly 600 MHz, and one from 36 inverters targeting roughly 300 MHz, each followed by a two-stage driver to drive the analog pads. Ring 1 is enabled via ui[0] and observed on uo[0], while ring 2 is enabled via ui[1] and observed on uo[1]. Testing requires an oscilloscope to measure the attenuated analog output, and the documentation notes that the 300 MHz oscillator had a missing contact in TT08 and was fixed for TT09. The design is notable for being a transistor-level analog oscillator experiment with known silicon issues.

results.summary_before: The Styler chip manipulates 16x16 character glyph bitmaps based on text mode attributes such as bold, faint, italic, underline, and blink. It has registers for scanline, control, bitmap, and attributes, and it interfaces via 8 bidirectional data pins and several control inputs. The typical use involves writing a scanline number, reading back a logical scanline, and then manipulating bitmap halves to apply visual effects. The chip is intended as part of a larger text mode video display hardware system, and testing is covered by provided test scripts.
